extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students / readers learning calculus and introductory analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Expository and pedagogical rules, definitions, and criteria used in a calculus/introductory analysis textbook for defining concepts (derivative, integral, series), proving properties (differentiability, convergence), and applying techniques (logarithmic differentiation, Taylor expansions, modeling with differential equations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logarithmic differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: For a product P(x)=f1(x) f2(x) ... fn(x), D(log P(x)) = D(log f1(x)) + ... + D(log fn(x)), and hence P'(x)/P(x) = f1'(x)/f1(x) + ... + fn'(x)/fn(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logarithmic differentiation to simplify differentiation of products, especially when factors are themselves complicated (examples given: x(x+1)...(x+n), x e^{-x}). The formula follows from differentiating log P(x) and the chain rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral representation of log(1+x)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from dy/dz = 1/z with z=1+x and then use the fundamental theorem of calculus. This integral representation can be used as the basis for obtaining series expansions by substituting a series for 1/(1+u) and integrating term-by-term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric series substitution and remainder control
rubrics_metrics.description: 1/(1+u) can be expanded as a finite geometric series 1 - u + u^2 - ... + (-1)^{n} u^{n} + remainder R_n (with explicit form of remainder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert the finite geometric series into the integral for log(1+x) and integrate term-by-term; choose domain -1 < x ≤ 1 (x = +1 included, x = -1 excluded) and argue that the remainder R_n tends to zero as n→∞ under these domain conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successive derivatives of exponential functions
rubrics_metrics.description: All successive derivatives of e^{x} (and e^{-x} etc.) have the form e^{x} multiplied by a polynomial in x; the nth derivative of e^{cx} times algebraic factors has a polynomial factor of specified degree (examples: degree 2n−2 in one starred exercise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction and product/chain rules to show the stated polynomial factor structure; this guides expectations about complexity of repeated differentiation and is useful for finding maxima/minima and higher derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous compounding limit (exponential growth law)
rubrics_metrics.description: If interest r is compounded n times per unit time, (1 + r/n)^{n} → e^{r} as n→∞, so continuous compounding gives growth factor e^{rt}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the limit definition of e^z = lim_{n→∞} (1+z/n)^n. Apply to compound interest problems to model continuous processes and compute doubling times via logarithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling damped vibrations with ODE
rubrics_metrics.description: For a mass attached to a spring with Hooke's law restoring force −k x and friction proportional to velocity −r x', Newton's law gives m x'' + r x' + k x = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differential equation models many mechanical and electrical vibrating systems; deriving the ODE from force balance is an expected modeling step and leads to classification of solutions (damped/undamped/overdamped etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical definition of derivative and differentiability
rubrics_metrics.description: A function y=f(x) is differentiable at x if the difference quotient (f(x+h)-f(x))/h has a single limit f'(x) as h→0 from either side; differentiability implies continuity but continuity does not imply differentiability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on geometric intuition alone; differentiability must be proved or assumed. Use explicit difference-quotient limits for verification; be aware of 'corner' and oscillatory counterexamples (e.g., functions involving |x| or x sin(1/x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of non-differentiability and how to test
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions like y=x+|x| or y=|x| have corners and fail to have derivatives at certain points. The function x sin(1/x), defined 0 at x=0, is continuous everywhere but its derivative at 0 does not exist due to oscillating difference quotients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the difference quotient and examine one-sided limits or oscillation bounds to test for differentiability. Provide exercises constructing such functions and locating nondifferentiable points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of integral as limit of Riemann sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Form sums S_n = Σ f(ξ_j) Δx_j over a partition a=x_0<x_1<...<x_n=b with arbitrary sample points ξ_j in intervals; as n→∞ and mesh→0, S_n tends to a limit A independent of partition choice when f is continuous; define A = ∫_a^b f(x) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analytic definition replaces vague geometric notions of 'area under a curve'; existence of the limit requires proof (standard in rigorous texts). Use this framework to justify integral properties and the fundamental theorem of calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications of the integral: work and arc length
rubrics_metrics.description: Work done by a variable force f(x) moving from a to b is ∫_a^b f(x) dx. Arc length of y=f(x), with continuous derivative f'(x), is L = ∫_a^b sqrt(1 + (f'(x))^2) dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive these formulas by approximating with stepwise-constant forces or inscribed polygonal approximations to the curve, then passing to the limit. Note conditions required (e.g., continuity of f' for rectifiability) and that explicit evaluation may be difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orders of magnitude and comparison of sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: For sequences a_n,b_n→∞, say b_n has higher order than a_n if a_n/b_n → 0. In particular exponentials (a^n with a>1) grow faster than any power n^s, and log n grows slower than any power n^s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use limits of ratios and root tests (taking s-th roots) to compare growth; this provides a precise language for 'faster' and 'slower' growth and supports asymptotic reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic of log(n!) via integral comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: P_n = log 2 + log 3 + ... + log n satisfies P_n ∼ n log n as n→∞; bounds obtained by comparing the sum to integrals of log x give n log n − n + 1 < P_n < (n+1) log(n+1) − n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare discrete sums with integrals (areas under curves) to obtain two-sided bounds that squeeze the ratio P_n/(n log n)→1. This method exemplifies a standard technique in asymptotic estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite series and convergence via partial sums
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinite series Σ b_k converges to s iff the sequence of partial sums S_n = Σ_{k=1}^n b_k has a limit s as n→∞; otherwise it diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partial sums to test convergence; provide examples of convergent alternating series, conditionally convergent series (e.g., alternating harmonic), and divergent series where partial sums oscillate or grow without bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power series expansions and domains of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions can be expanded in power series f(x)=c_0 + c_1 x + c_2 x^2 + ...; specific examples include geometric series 1/(1−x)=1+x+x^2+... valid for |x|<1, log(1+x)=x−x^2/2+... valid for −1<x<1, and expansions for sin x, cos x, e^x valid for all real x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about intervals/radii of convergence for each expansion; substitutions (e.g., x→−x or manipulations) must respect convergence regions. Use these expansions for computation and approximation where valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor series and coefficient formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has derivatives of all orders near 0 and if term-by-term differentiation of the power series is permitted, then the Taylor series coefficients satisfy n! c_n = f^{(n)}(0), giving f(x) = Σ_{n=0}^∞ f^{(n)}(0)/n! x^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook presents a plausibility derivation but notes precise conditions for validity (convergence to f and interchange of limits/differentiation) require more careful theorems; nevertheless, compute coefficients by evaluating derivatives at the expansion point when conditions are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating series error bound
rubrics_metrics.description: For an alternating series whose terms decrease in magnitude to 0, the error committed by truncating after a given term does not exceed the magnitude of the first omitted term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this bound for numerical computation (example: computing sin 1° from its Taylor series) to choose truncation so that the remainder is below desired tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newton's generalized binomial theorem and convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: (1+x)^a = 1 + a x + (a(a−1)/2!) x^2 + ... as an infinite series when a is not an integer; this series is valid for −1 < x < 1 (convergent there, divergent for |x|>1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand binomial coefficients for non-integer a (generalized coefficients) and restrict use to the radius of convergence; avoid applying the expansion outside its domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's formula and formal derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Euler's formula cos x + i sin x = e^{ix} can be suggested formally via De Moivre's formula or by substituting z=ix into the series for e^z and separating real and imaginary parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook emphasizes these arguments are formal and not fully rigorous in the absence of complex-function theory; rigorous justification requires the theory of functions of a complex variable and careful analysis of series convergence for complex arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence domain determined by complex singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Convergence behavior of power series can be explained by studying the function for complex values: divergence at a point often reflects a pole/singularity in the complex plane; radius of convergence is up to the nearest singularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: geometric series 1/(1+x) yields divergent termwise series at x=1 producing 1−1+1−1+..., and divergence for |x|>1 can be explained by the singularity at x=−1 (and in complex plane at x=i for related expansions). Use complex analysis for rigorous radius-of-convergence arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic series divergence and grouping proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The harmonic series Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/n diverges (partial sums grow without bound); grouping terms shows partial sums exceed any finite bound (e.g., S_{2^m} > 1 + m/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inequalities/grouping to show that partial sums can be made arbitrarily large; contrast with series Σ 1/n^s which converge for s>1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeta function definition and Euler product
rubrics_metrics.description: For s>1, ζ(s) = Σ_{n=1}^∞ n^{-s} converges and admits the Euler product ζ(s) = ∏_{p prime} (1 − p^{-s})^{−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive Euler product formally by multiplying geometric-series factors (1−p^{-s})^{−1} for each prime p and using unique prime factorization; note the product and series identities are valid for s>1 and tie analytic behavior to distribution of primes.
